It was copied and recognized by Zhang Tingji when he was sixty-three years old.　　Inscription of five seals of Zhang Tingji: "Zhang Shuwei", "Tingji", "Xinhuangli", "Baolang", and "Zhang Shuwei", "Zhang Shuwei Zhongdingxue".　　This is recorded from the inscription of the Shi Song tripod. Shi Song Ding is a late Western Zhou period food vessel. The inscription on the inner wall of the vessel has 6 lines and 63 characters, which reads that Shi Song was ordered by the king of Zhou to visit the land of Su and was given a gift by the king of Zhou. Zhang Tingji was not only a scholar of jinshi, but also a famous collector of bells, cinges and rituals, of which the Shisong tripod is one. The collection of this tripod is described in detail in Zhang's self-title at the end of the page. This tripod is now in the Shanghai Museum.　　This work was written in 1830, when Zhang Tingji was 63 years old. Compared with the original inscription, the shape of the inscription is quite similar, but due to the different writing materials and tools, the strokes are soft and flexible, making the turn flexible and showing the changes in the weight and intensity of the ink. This is an aesthetic realm of calligraphy pioneered by Qing Dynasty calligraphers, and Zhang Tingji's work is a successful example.
